content: The Pulse Polio campaign invites individuals to take over the editorial responsibilities for this topic. Interested parties can apply to become the Editor-in-Chief for the entire topic or an Associate Editor-in-Chief for one of the subtopics. Applicants are required to email their interest and include their CV or a biographical sketch. Pulse Polio is an immunization initiative launched by the Government of India in 1994 with the goal of eradicating poliomyelitis (polio) in the country. The campaign involves the annual vaccination of all children under the age of five with the Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV). This vaccine contains a live, attenuated virus that colonizes the gastrointestinal tract. By doing so, it competitively inhibits the wild, disease-causing poliovirus. This mechanism not only prevents severe infection in the vaccinated individual but also halts the transmission of the wild poliovirus to others. Since the poliovirus cannot survive outside a host for more than two weeks, its eradication is theoretically achievable, leading to the elimination of poliomyelitis. The campaign has been highly successful, with a dramatic reduction in polio cases in India. In 1994, there were 4,791 reported cases of polio. This number decreased to 2,489 in 1997, 1,600 in 2002, 225 in 2003, and 135 in 2004. However, critics argue that the campaign has, at times, significantly encroached upon other essential public health services, particularly during periods when healthcare resources were already limited.
